bp: A web application is a living surface made of forms, links, buttons, request parameters, cookies, pages, and server replies. Security testers want to know whether unusual inputs can make that surface reveal a real vulnerability, but in many practical settings they cannot inspect the server code. They only see the outside: send a request, receive a page, error, redirect, status, or other response. This paper serves that setting. It asks how to test a web application as a closed box, where the inside remains hidden, without falling back to blind guessing. Zelda is built for vulnerability discovery, not just for making pages respond differently. The need is concrete: if a tester can turn visible web responses into guidance, then the test can explore more of the application and spend more effort where a weakness may actually be reachable. The reported outcome, 182 vulnerabilities across real applications and benchmark sets plus 29 CVE assignments in the wild, shows that the task is operational security work.
wh: The hard part is that web fuzzing has to search an enormous input space with very little direct feedback. A tester can vary field values, URL parameters, request order, headers, and page actions, but most combinations are harmless or never reach interesting server logic. In open or partly open testing, code coverage can tell the tester which internal paths were touched. In closed-box web testing, the abstract says that feedback mechanism is missing. The tester sees responses, but not the program branches that created them. The second difficulty is exploitation. It is not enough to find that some page changed after an input. Vulnerability identification can be shallow: the tool may notice surface novelty without knowing how to push that behavior toward a security failure. So the same system must solve two different jobs. It must first map reachable behavior, then shift from broad exploration into focused attempts to expose vulnerabilities.
naive: A smart beginner would build a web fuzzer that sends many strange strings into every visible input field, records crashes or obvious error pages, and keeps going until time runs out. That can find simple bugs, especially when one malformed value directly triggers an obvious failure. It fails for the setting described here because closed-box web applications rarely reveal their internal path structure. Random mutations may revisit the same page logic again and again while leaving other paths untouched. Even when a response changes, the beginner tool may treat every change as equally interesting. That wastes effort on cosmetic differences and gives too little attention to inputs that should be exploited more deeply for actual vulnerability identification.
ap: The paper's central move is to treat the web response as a substitute instrument panel. Zelda cannot read the server's code path, so it infers feedback signals from what the application sends back. In plain terms, it asks whether a response carries evidence that the input reached something different: a different page shape, content change, error behavior, or other observable sign supported by the closed-box response. Those inferred signals guide the next inputs instead of letting generation stay blind. Zelda then separates input generation into two roles. One role is path exploration: produce inputs meant to reach more parts of the in-page behavior and application logic. The other role is exploitation: once exploration has exposed a promising stage, produce inputs meant to turn shallow signs into vulnerability findings. The coordination between these roles is the method's key practical idea.
mech: The mechanism begins with a web application that the tester can interact with only from the outside. The inputs are web-facing actions and values: requests, parameters, form entries, and other data that can be supplied through the application's visible interface. Zelda sends candidate inputs and observes the responses. Because the tool is closed-box, it cannot ask the program which internal branch ran. Instead, it transforms each response into feedback signals. The abstract does not list the exact signals, so the grounded statement is narrower: Zelda derives guidance from observable web responses in the testing environment. Those signals are used to decide whether the current input opened new behavior or merely repeated known surface behavior. During an exploration stage, the system favors generation that broadens coverage of in-page code and reachable paths. When the stage indicates that a behavior is worth deeper probing, Zelda coordinates a second generation strategy aimed at exploitation, meaning it tries inputs that make vulnerability identification more effective rather than only increasing response variety. Each round therefore has a loop: generate an input, send it to the application, observe the response, infer feedback, choose the next stage or strategy, and generate again. The output is a set of discovered vulnerabilities, supported in the abstract by evaluation on 15 real-world applications and nine benchmark sets.
math: The mathematical idea is guided search under partial observation. Search means choosing one candidate input after another from a huge set of possible inputs. Partial observation means the system does not see the true internal state of the web application; it sees only the response. Zelda's feedback signals turn those responses into a scoring language for the search. A score is not truth about the whole program. It is a practical sign that one input taught more than another, perhaps because the response suggests a different path or a vulnerability-relevant behavior. This is also a budget problem. The fuzzer has limited time, so it must decide whether to spend the next attempt exploring new territory or exploiting a suspicious place it has already reached. That is a form of optimization, in the plain sense of defining what counts as useful progress and repeatedly choosing actions that reduce wasted trials. The two strategies express a tradeoff: breadth versus depth. Breadth tries to avoid missing hidden paths; depth tries to avoid stopping at shallow response changes. The math fits because closed-box web testing is not about proving all inputs safe. It is about using weak observable evidence to steer a costly search toward inputs more likely to expose real security failures.
dots: Within this dataset, Zelda sits beside other security and reliability papers that ask how to expose hidden failures when the internal truth is hard to see. WasmDiff, the WebAssembly differential fuzzing paper, compares two executions that should agree; Zelda instead has only one closed web system and must infer useful clues from its responses. SemFuzz, the protocol fuzzing paper in the repo data, uses protocol semantics from specifications to make test cases meaningful; Zelda uses response-derived feedback because web application internals and precise rules are not available. The broader conference connection is ranking and search. Like retrieval systems that choose which documents to inspect next, Zelda chooses which inputs deserve the next attempt. Like anomaly and security papers, it treats unusual observations as possible evidence but must separate harmless novelty from risk. Its theme, Web fuzzing, is therefore a specialized case of guided exploration under uncertainty.
ww: Zelda should improve over blind closed-box fuzzing because it extracts direction from the only evidence the setting allows. A random fuzzer treats many inputs as interchangeable until one visibly breaks something. Zelda instead asks whether the response implies that the input changed what part of the application was exercised. That helps because web applications are not uniform surfaces. Some fields may be heavily sanitized, some actions may lead to deeper code, and some paths may only become reachable after earlier interactions. Feedback lets the tool stop spending equal effort everywhere. The second reason is the split between exploration and exploitation. If a tool only explores, it may collect many response differences without turning them into confirmed vulnerabilities. If it only exploits early, it may dig deeply in the wrong place and miss other paths. Zelda's coordinated strategies let the testing behavior change with the stage: first broaden the map, then push promising areas harder. The evaluation results in the abstract support this explanation: the feedback mechanism and strategies outperform six web fuzzers and uncover vulnerabilities in both controlled and wild settings.
po: The payoff is a more practical closed-box web vulnerability finder. Zelda gives testers a way to guide fuzzing even when they cannot instrument the server or inspect its code. In the reported evaluation, it is tested on 15 real-world applications and nine benchmark sets, uncovers 182 vulnerabilities, and outperforms six existing web fuzzers. The wild deployment result is especially important: previously unreported vulnerabilities received 29 CVE assignments. That means the method is not only producing artificial test-case wins; it is finding security issues serious enough to enter the public vulnerability record.
limits: The abstract does not prove that Zelda finds every vulnerability or that response-derived feedback always mirrors internal coverage. Some server paths may produce similar responses even when the internal behavior differs, while harmless changes may look more interesting than they are. The method assumes observable web responses contain enough signal to guide search and that the staged choice between exploration and exploitation is well matched to the application. Its evidence covers 15 real-world applications, nine benchmark sets, and wild discoveries, but those do not cover every web stack, authentication pattern, rate limit, hidden state, or vulnerability class. The abstract also reports discovery counts, not automatic repair.
